reason: The sources provide enough multi-sourced atomic facts to build a high-impact, true 45-second script about Stanislav Petrov.
story: On September 26, 1983, at the height of Cold War tensions, Soviet early-warning satellites suddenly detected a US intercontinental ballistic missile launch, followed quickly by four more. Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov sat at his console in a secret bunker near Moscow. Soviet doctrine demanded an immediate, compulsory nuclear counterattack upon receiving such a warning. But Petrov hesitated. He suspected the new system might be malfunctioning, reasoning that a genuine US first strike would involve hundreds of simultaneous missiles, not just five. Disobeying protocol, he reported the alert as a false alarm rather than notifying top commanders. Twenty-three minutes later, with no impacts recorded, he realized he was right. The satellites had mistaken sunlight reflecting off high-altitude clouds for missile exhaust. By trusting his gut and stalling the chain of command, Petrov single-handedly prevented a catastrophic retaliatory nuclear war.
angle: A single Soviet duty officer prevented a full-scale nuclear war by intentionally disobeying protocol and dismissing a computer-verified missile attack as a glitch.

claims.claim: Stanislav Petrov was a lieutenant colonel in the Soviet Air Defence Forces and the duty officer at the Serpukhov-15 command center.
The early warning computer system reported four additional incoming missiles shortly after the first.
Petrov decided to treat the warning as a false alarm instead of immediately relaying the warning up the chain of command.
Subsequent investigation determined the false alarm was caused by a rare alignment of sunlight on high-altitude clouds and the satellites' Molniya orbits.
Petrov reasoned that a real US first strike would involve a massive, all-out onslaught of hundreds of missiles rather than just five.
On 1 September 1983, the Soviet military shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007 after it strayed into Soviet airspace, killing all 269 people aboard.
Petrov was later questioned by his superiors and received an official reprimand for mistakes made in his logbook or paperwork.
The incident did not become publicly known until 1998 with the publication of General Yuri Votintsev's memoirs.
Petrov died on 19 May 2017 at the age of 77 in Fryazino, a suburb of Moscow.
Petrov received international recognition later in life, including the Dresden Peace Prize and an award from the Association of World Citizens.

disputed: Accounts differ on whether Petrov notified his superiors or completely withheld the warning up the chain of command; scripts should follow the primary account that he reported a system malfunction instead of forwarding an attack warning.
Accounts vary on whether Petrov received initial praise or a promised reward alongside his reprimand; scripts can state he faced intense questioning and an official reprimand over paperwork errors.
